Testimony Neither For Nor Against LD 2210
An Act to Clarify Board of Environmental Protection Procedures Regarding Appeals of Licensing or Permitting Decisions of the Commissioner of Environmental Protection
February 25, 2026
Senator Tepler, Representative Doudera, and Honorable Members of the Environment and Natural Resources Committee;
On behalf of the American Council of Engineering Companies of Maine (ACEC of Maine), please find below our comments neither for nor against LD 2210, An Act to Clarify Board of Environmental Protection Procedures Regarding Appeals of Licensing or Permitting Decisions of the Commissioner of Environmental Protection.
ACEC of Maine is primarily interested in better understanding the intent of this bill with respect to appellants who are not directly impacted by a project. Specifically, we wish to understand whether an appellant must hold some kind of standing or demonstrate an interest in the project being permitted or licensing being issued. We understand that some aspects of this bill may seek to codify existing policy at the DEP or BEP, but we caution that codifying a policy that widely allows anyone to appeal a decision may create unintended consequences.
We recognize that DEP is working hard to streamline its processes and expedite procedures. We are concerned that if anyone who is aggrieved but not actually impacted by a project is permitted to weigh in as an appellant, it may clog up the docket at the BEP.
We would encourage the ENR Committee to consider putting parameters around who may appeal a decision and what specific interest they must demonstrate. While a specific legal standard of standing may not be appropriate, we do think some guardrails around who may appeal would help prevent frivolous appeals by individuals who will never be directly impacted by a proposed project.
ACEC is always happy to be a resource for the ENR Committee, and to answer any questions you may have about our experiences with appeals, our perspective on cautionary guidelines, and any other issue that may arise during your discussion on this bill and others.
Thank you for your consideration of this testimony.
Sincerely,
Elizabeth M. Frazier On behalf of ACEC of Maine

Senator Tepler, Representative Doudera, and members of the Environment and Natural
Resources Committee, my name is Luke Frankel, and I am the Staff Scientist at the Natural
Resources Council of Maine (NRCM). NRCM is a nonprofit, nonpartisan membership
organization dedicated to protecting, restoring, and conserving Maine's environment, now and
for future generations. I am here to testify neither for nor against LD 2210, An Act to Clarify
Board of Environmental Protection Procedures Regarding Appeals of Licensing or Permitting Decisions of the Commissioner of Environmental Protection.
As an environmental advocacy organization with nearly 20,000 members and supporters statewide and beyond, public involvement in legal, legislative, and regulatory processes is
critical to our work. We recognize, however, that the infrastructure to support this public
involvement is not free and does come with a cost. In this case, when it comes to issues like
rulemaking, appeals, or other proceedings before the Board of Environmental Protection (BEP), this cost comes in the form of Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) staff time.
We greatly appreciate all the work that DEP staff do to ensure that there is a transparent public process for proceedings before the BEP and believe that the current process sets a high standard that other governmental bodies should look to. We do agree that there are likely ways that this
process could be streamlined to save staff time without sacrificing public input.
One example of this, which is included within this bill, is prohibiting "interested persons" from
submitting supplemental evidence into the record as part of the BEP appeal process, which we do not oppose. DEP staff have stated that sifting through vast amounts of supplemental evidence submitted by people who are not direct parties to an appeal has cost them significant staff time
through the years. These entities would still be entitled to submit information into the record during any public comment periods prior to a final license or permit decision.
We would, however, like to propose a few amendments to the bill that would clarify current practices around_"interested persons" during appeals to the BEP under DEP's Chapter 2 rules.

proposed projects during the review of license applications, the Department supports L.D. 2210.
The proposed amendments to Section 4 would clarify what constitutes the record the Board uses when deciding appeals. This new language is based on an existing section
of the Department's Chapter 2 rule that outlines appeal procedures. While a statutory change is not required for the Board to maintain its current practice regarding the record used in appeals, adding this detail in statute would add clarity, especially given that the existing statute provides for consideration of supplemental evidence.
The first substantive proposed amendment to Section 4(A) would specify that each appellant must include all the information required to be submitted to the Board when an appeal is filed. Although a statutory change is not required for the Board to maintain its current practice under Chapter 2 to require each appellant to include the minimum
information necessary for the Board to understand the merits of the appeal and to determine whether the appellant has standing to bring the appeal to the Board, the
proposed amendment would support this Chapter 2 requirement and strengthen the
Board's authority to dismiss appeals that fail to provide the required contents.
The second substantive proposed amendment to Section 4(A) would clarify who is
permitted to submit proposed supplemental evidence to the Board. Typically, the Board
makes its decision on an appeal based on the same record of information that was
available to and considered by the DEP Commissioner before the license decision was
issued. However, the statute allows the Board to consider supplemental evidence that
was not considered by the Commissioner, provided the supplemental evidence is relevant and material to the appeal and was presented to the Department at the earliest possible time. The Department interprets the current statute to allow persons who are neither the licensee nor the appellant--including people who would not have standing to
appeal the decision--to offer supplemental evidence during an appeal proceeding. Anytime a person offers proposed supplemental evidence, it slows the appeal process.

L.D. 2210 An Act to Clarify Board of Environmental Protection Procedures Regarding Appeals of Licensing or Permitting Decisions of the Commissioner of Environmental Protections Testimony of: Bill Hinkel, DEP Public Hearing: February 25, 2026 Page 3 of 4
As currently structured, this provision could be abused to intentionally delay a Board decision on appeal, which is wasteful of Department resources and reduces regulatory
certainty for licensees. Furthermore, allowing a person to submit proposed supplemental evidence to the Department during an appeal proceeding discourages participation in the licensing process while the application is pending before the
Commissioner. L.D. 2210 clarifies that the appellant and the licensee may submit
proposed supplemental evidence. lf the Legislature is satisfied with the current
structure, which may result in licensees having to potentially wait well over a year to
have a license upheld, no changes to this aspect of the statute are necessary. However,
if the intention is to make the overall permitting process faster and allow licensees to proceed with major investments, the Legislature should make the changes proposed in
L.D. 2210.
The last substantive proposed amendment to Section 4(A) adds language incorporating
the Board's long-held practice of allowing the licensee to submit a written response to the merits of the appeal. Although a statutory change is not required for the Board to maintain its current practice under Chapter 2, clarifying this due process right of the licensee in statute strengthens the provision that is currently only specified in rule.
The other proposed amendments included in L.D. 2210 are for language consistency and conciseness and are supported by the Department.
The Department suggests additional language changes for consistency and clarity regarding references in the statute to the record on appeal. I have circulated to the Committee a mark-up of L.D. 2210 with those additional proposed changes shown in double strikethrough and double underline.
In conclusion, L.D. 2210 would result in important and helpful clarifications regarding the Board's appeal procedure, incorporate practices of the Board that are outlined in the

DEP's Chapter 2 rule, encourage early participation in DEP licensing proceedings, and
ensure due process and improve regulatory certainty for appellants and licensees.
Thank you for the opportunity to provide testimony. l am available to answer questions
of the Committee, both now and at the work session.

SUMMARY
This bill, which is reported out by the Joint Standing Committee on Environment and Natural Resources pursuant to the Maine Revised Statutes, Title 3, section 955, subsection 4, implements recommendations resulting from the committee's review of the Board of Environmental Protection under the State Government Evaluation Act. The bill amends procedures of the Board of Environmental Protection regarding appeals of licensing or permitting decisions of the Commissioner of Environmental Protection as follows.
1. It specifies the composition of the record to be considered by the board in deciding an appeal of a final license or permit decision of the commissioner.

2. It clarifies that an appellant to a final license or permit decision must include in the appeal all information required by rule of the board.
3. lt clarifies the persons that may offer proposed supplemental evidence in an appeal proceeding before the board and the circumstances under which that evidence may be submitted to the board and provides
that it is the chair of the board that determines the admissibility of that evidence. 4. It codifies a longstanding practice of the Department of Environmental Protection to allow a licensee
or permittee, if the licensee or permittee is not an appellant to a final license or permit decision, to submit to the board a written response to the merits of the appeal.
The committee has not taken a position on the substance of the bill and, by reporting this bill out, the committee is not suggesting and does not intend to suggest that it agrees or disagrees with any aspect of this bill.
